chunks.text: PawPals Pet Clinic - Cat Nutrition Guide Cats are obligate carnivores. They need a diet high in animal protein and cannot get all their nutrients from plant food. Kittens Kittens up to 12 months old should eat food labelled for growth. Feed 3 to 4 small meals each day until 6 months of age, then reduce to 2 meals per day. Adult cats Most adult cats do well on 2 measured meals per day. Check the feeding chart on the food package and adjust to keep a healthy body weight. You should be able to

feeding chart on the food package and adjust to keep a healthy body weight. You should be able to feel your cat's ribs under a thin layer of fat. Senior cats Cats older than 10 years may need food with easy-to-digest protein and controlled phosphorus. Ask the clinic before switching to a senior or kidney support diet. Wet and dry food Wet food adds water to the diet and can help urinary health. Dry food is convenient and can be left out for a short time. A mix of both is common. Change foods

Dry food is convenient and can be left out for a short time. A mix of both is common. Change foods slowly over 7 to 10 days by mixing the new food with the old food in growing amounts. Water Always provide fresh water. Many cats prefer a wide, shallow bowl or a water fountain. Foods to avoid Never feed onions, garlic, chocolate, grapes, raisins, alcohol or caffeine. Milk can cause stomach upset in many adult cats.

PawPals Pet Clinic - Dog Vaccination Schedule Purpose This care sheet explains when puppies and adult dogs should receive core and non-core vaccines at PawPals Pet Clinic. Puppy schedule Puppies should receive their first vaccine at 6 to 8 weeks of age. Boosters are given every 3 to 4 weeks until the puppy is 16 weeks old. The core vaccine covers distemper, parvovirus, adenovirus and parainfluenza. The rabies vaccine is given at 12 to 16 weeks, as required by local law. Adult dogs Adult dogs

The rabies vaccine is given at 12 to 16 weeks, as required by local law. Adult dogs Adult dogs need a core booster one year after the final puppy vaccine, then every 3 years. Rabies boosters follow the schedule printed on the rabies certificate, usually every 1 to 3 years. Non-core vaccines Bordetella (kennel cough), leptospirosis and Lyme vaccines are recommended based on lifestyle. Dogs that visit boarding kennels, groomers or dog parks should have the Bordetella vaccine at least 7 days

visit boarding kennels, groomers or dog parks should have the Bordetella vaccine at least 7 days before the visit. After vaccination Mild tiredness, a small lump at the injection site and a slight drop in appetite can last up to 48 hours. Call the clinic right away if your dog has facial swelling, repeated vomiting, hives or trouble breathing, because these can be signs of an allergic reaction. Keep your pet's vaccination record in a safe place and bring it to every visit.

PawPals Pet Clinic - Flea and Tick Prevention Fleas and ticks can cause itching, skin infections, anaemia and serious diseases. Prevention is easier than treatment. Year-round protection Use a veterinarian-approved preventive every month for the whole year. Fleas can survive indoors in cold weather, and ticks can be active on warm winter days. Product options Options include monthly spot-on treatments, chewable tablets and long-acting collars. Our vets will recommend a product based on your

chewable tablets and long-acting collars. Our vets will recommend a product based on your pet's species, weight and age. Safety warning for cats Never use dog flea products on cats. Some dog products contain permethrin, which is toxic to cats and can cause tremors or seizures. Contact the clinic immediately if this happens. Checking your pet After walks in grass or wooded areas, check your pet's head, ears, neck, armpits and between the toes for ticks. Remove a tick with fine-tipped tweezers by

head, ears, neck, armpits and between the toes for ticks. Remove a tick with fine-tipped tweezers by grasping it close to the skin and pulling straight out. Clean the area and keep the tick in a sealed container in case the vet wants to see it. Treating the home If you find fleas, wash pet bedding in hot water, vacuum carpets and furniture often, and treat all pets in the household at the same time. PawPals Pet Clinic - Pet Dental Care More than 80 percent of dogs and cats show signs of dental disease by age 3. Bad dental health can lead to pain, tooth loss and infections that spread to the heart and kidneys. Daily brushing Brush your pet's teeth daily if possible, or at least 3 times a week. Use a pet toothpaste only. Human toothpaste contains fluoride and xylitol, which can be harmful to pets. Start slowly by letting your pet lick the toothpaste, then introduce a soft brush. Dental chews

Start slowly by letting your pet lick the toothpaste, then introduce a soft brush. Dental chews and diets Dental chews and special diets can help reduce plaque. Choose products with the VOHC seal of acceptance, and avoid very hard items such as bones and antlers, because they can break teeth. Professional cleaning Most pets benefit from a professional dental cleaning once a year. The procedure is done under anaesthesia so the vet can clean below the gum line and take dental X-rays. Warning signs Bad breath, red or bleeding gums, drooling, dropping food, pawing at the mouth, or a reluctance to eat hard food are signs your pet needs a dental check. Book a dental check If you notice any of these signs, book an exam with the clinic. Early treatment is cheaper and safer than waiting.

PawPals Pet Clinic - When to Seek Emergency Care Some symptoms need urgent veterinary care. If you are unsure, call the clinic first. If the clinic is closed, go to the nearest emergency animal hospital. Go immediately if your pet has: Difficulty breathing or constant coughing, collapse or inability to stand, seizures lasting more than 3 minutes, heavy bleeding that does not stop after 5 minutes of pressure, a swollen hard belly with unproductive retching, suspected poisoning, or a straining

of pressure, a swollen hard belly with unproductive retching, suspected poisoning, or a straining male cat that cannot pass urine. Common poisons Chocolate, xylitol sweetener, grapes, raisins, onions, human medicines, rat poison and antifreeze are dangerous to pets. Do not try to make your pet vomit unless a vet tells you to. Call the same day if your pet has: Vomiting or diarrhoea lasting more than 24 hours, refusal to eat for more than a day, limping that does not improve, eye injuries, or a

than 24 hours, refusal to eat for more than a day, limping that does not improve, eye injuries, or a wound that looks infected. What to tell us Share your pet's species, age, weight, the symptoms, when they started and anything your pet may have eaten. If possible, bring the packaging of any suspected poison. Be prepared Keep the clinic number and the emergency hospital address saved in your phone.

PawPals Pet Clinic - Puppy House Training Tips House training takes patience and a steady routine. Most puppies learn the basics in 4 to 6 months, but some small breeds take longer. Set a routine Take your puppy outside first thing in the morning, after every meal, after naps, after play and right before bed. Young puppies may need to go out every 1 to 2 hours. Use one spot Bring your puppy to the same outdoor spot each time. The familiar smell helps them understand what to do. Stay with them

the same outdoor spot each time. The familiar smell helps them understand what to do. Stay with them and use a calm cue word such as "go potty". Reward right away Give a small treat and praise within 3 seconds of finishing outside. Rewards given later will not connect to the behaviour. Handle accidents calmly Do not punish or scold your puppy for accidents. Clean the spot with an enzyme cleaner to remove the smell. If you catch your puppy in the act, calmly say "oops" and take them outside.

Crate training A crate that is just big enough to stand and turn around in can help, because dogs avoid soiling their sleeping area. Do not leave a puppy in a crate longer than they can hold it. A rule of thumb is one hour for each month of age, plus one.
